meta.title: Who really said "There are two ways to conquer and enslave a nation. One is by the sword. The other is by debt"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not John Adams. The sword-and-debt line has no source in his writings; Barry Popik's earliest listing is a 2002 Usenet post. Snopes rates it False.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There are two ways to conquer and enslave a nation. One is by the sword. The other is by debt'?
meta.ogDescription: Pinned on John Adams, but the Adams Papers editors found no evidence he wrote it. The earliest listing Popik gives is a 2002 Usenet post.

answer.label: Not John Adams — an internet-era misattribution
answer.authorDates: Earliest listing found by Barry Popik: a Usenet post of 31 August 2002
answer.sourceLine: No letter, speech or diary entry by John Adams contains this line. Etymologist Barry Popik finds “no record that Adams ever said it” and lists a 31 August 2002 Usenet post as his earliest example. The editor-in-chief of the Adams Papers has said the sentiment fits Adams, but her team has “found no direct evidence that Adams ever wrote it.”

source.heading: Where the line actually turns up

docMeta.dd: Usenet newsgroup alt.appalachian, 31 August 2002 (as transcribed by Barry Popik)

No direct evidence, per the Adams Papers editor-in-chief (as reported by Snopes)

source.excerpt: “There are two ways to conquer and enslave a nation. One is by the sword, the other is by debt.” — John Adams
trail: Barry Popik (entry dated December 8, 2009) writes that “there is no record that Adams ever said it” and that the quotation “appears in print from only about 2002.” The earliest item he lists is a 31 August 2002 alt.appalachian Usenet post. Popik’s citations ↗

Snopes (2023) rated the attribution False. It relays a statement given to CheckYourFact by Sara Martin, editor-in-chief of the Adams Papers: the sentiment “is in keeping with John Adams,” but “we have found no direct evidence that Adams ever wrote it.” Snopes fact check ↗
Wikiquote leaves the line off its John Adams page. It appears only on the page’s Talk page, in a list headed “Unsourced”, awaiting a reliable source. Talk:John Adams ↗

What Adams actually said about debt, in his First Annual Message of November 22, 1797: “The consequences arising from the continual accumulation of public debts in other countries ought to admonish us to be careful to prevent their growth in our own.” It is a warning about debt, with nothing about conquest or slavery. Avalon Project text ↗
source.excerptNote: This is the wording in the 31 August 2002 alt.appalachian post, the earliest example in Barry Popik’s entry ↗. Later copies swap “nation” for “country” and sometimes add the date “1826”. Popik notes that 1826 is the year Adams died, and there is no evidence he said it then.

source.rightsNote: The wording can’t be traced to any identifiable author or published work. Its earliest known appearance is an anonymous 2002 Usenet post, so quotle.info makes no copyright claim either way. Adams’s genuine 1797 First Annual Message is public domain, but it does not contain this line.

author.name: John Adams
author.heading: The man it's pinned on
author.metaLine: 1735–1826 · Second President of the United States (1797–1801)
author.bio: John Adams was a Founding Father, the first Vice President, and the second President of the United States. He left a vast record of letters, diaries and state papers, and none of it is known to contain the sword-and-debt line. His real views on debt appear in plainer terms in his 1797 First Annual Message.

misattribution.heading: One anonymous line, several famous names
misattribution.intro: With no real source behind it, the sword-and-debt line has drifted between names and picked up a date it never had.

items.why: Credited to Adams in online posts since at least 2002, then in books and newspaper letters. Popik finds “no record that Adams ever said it”, and Snopes reports the Adams Papers editors found no direct evidence. Popik ↗
A tweet of July 22, 2011 tacked on “1826”. Popik notes Adams died that year and there is no evidence he said it then. Popik ↗
A 4 November 2008 article in the Cowichan News Leader Pictorial (Duncan, BC) credited the same line to Madison. Popik ↗
The quote site QuotePark credits the “country” version to the sixth president, with no source of any kind. QuotePark ↗

An anonymous blog commenter claimed the line was “fabricated whole-cloth by lawyer Ellen Brown” (blog ↗). Popik does quote it from her 2008 book Web of Debt, but he also lists Usenet posts from 2002 and 2004, so it was circulating before that book.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody knows who first wrote the sword-and-debt line. It surfaces in anonymous online posts from 2002 and has no basis in Adams’s writings. Snopes: False ↗

context.heading: Why it sticks to Adams
lead: The line spreads in arguments about national debt and banking, and a Founding Father’s name gives it weight. Snopes traced a January 2013 Facebook post carrying it under Adams’s name that drew more than 55,000 shares, and a 2023 meme that revived it. Snopes ↗

It is believable partly because Adams really did worry about debt. His 1797 First Annual Message warned that piling up public debt abroad “ought to admonish us to be careful to prevent their growth in our own.” But that is advice on public finance. The vivid sword-versus-debt framing and the talk of enslavement are not his. Avalon Project ↗
context.pull: “We have found no direct evidence that Adams ever wrote it.” — Sara Martin, Adams Papers, as reported by Snopes
